title: Large Deviations in Switching Diffusion: Dynamical Condensation and Diffusivity BBP Transition
authors: Mathis Guéneau, Timo Schorlepp, Satya N. Majumdar, Gregory Schehr
abstract: We consider a Brownian particle with position $x(t)$ whose diffusivity changes at Poissonian switching times, with each new value drawn independently from a bounded distribution $W(D)$. Assuming $W(D)\sim C(D_{\max}-D)^ν$ near its upper edge, we study the large-deviation regime $x(t)\simeq yt$ with $y = O(1)$ at large times, far beyond the typical diffusive scale. In a recent work Guéneau et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 067102 (2025), the rate function of the displacement was obtained through a renewal approach and it was shown to display several singularities. In this paper, we carry out a detailed study of the corresponding dynamical phase transitions and trajectory condensation. For moderate $y$, the imposed displacement is shared among $O(t)$ displacement increments accumulated during successive intervals between switches. Beyond a first threshold $y_-$, one interval produces an increment of order $t$ carrying a finite fraction of the total displacement, signaling dynamical condensation. For $ν>1$, a second threshold $y_+>y_-$ is reached when this macroscopic increment carries asymptotically the entire imposed displacement, whereas for $0<ν\leq1$ the two thresholds merge, $y_-=y_+$. In turn, the moment-generating function of $x(t)$ displays a complementary transition from collective contributions of many diffusivities to selection of states near $D_{\max}$. We show that this transition is governed by the same edge mechanism as the Baik-Ben Arous-Péché (BBP) transition, indicating that diffusivity selection and trajectory condensation are two manifestations of the same phenomenon. We validate our predictions for the dynamical condensation against numerical results from rare event sampling.
summary: This paper studies large deviations in a switching diffusion process, where the diffusion coefficient changes randomly over time. It identifies two distinct dynamical phase transitions: dynamical condensation and the Diffusivity BBP transition. The key finding is that these two phenomena are mathematically equivalent, providing a unified understanding of how the system selects extreme states of diffusivity over long timescales.
main_problem: The paper investigates the large-deviation behavior and dynamical phase transitions in a system where the diffusion coefficient of a Brownian particle switches randomly over time.
main_result: It establishes that the dynamical condensation transition and the Diffusivity BBP transition are two complementary manifestations of the same underlying physical mechanism governing diffusivity selection.
method: The analysis uses renewal theory, moment-generating functions, and analogies to equilibrium statistical mechanics to derive rate functions and identify critical thresholds based on the edge exponent of the diffusivity distribution.

Diffusion coefficient sample path D(t) which is piecewise constant, with values drawn independently from W(D), during time intervals Ti −Ti−1 ∼Exp(r). Right. Corresponding sample path of x(t) with this diffusion coefficient history D(t). We denote the total displacement per constant D segment by ∆xi = x(Ti)−x(Ti−1).

FIG. 2. Sketch of the SCGF Ψ(q) (left column), rate function I(y) (center column), and space-time diagrams of the SD displacement (right column), cf. Ref. [44]. Top row. Right edge exponent ν ∈(0, 1], where the SCGF dynamical phase transition is continuous. Bottom row. Right edge exponent ν > 1, where the SCGF dynamical phase transition is first order, and an intermediate coexistence region appears for the displacement.

FIG. 3. Phase diagrams of the SCGF Ψ(q) (left) and rate function I(y) (right) for the example W(D) = (ν + 1)(1 −D)ν of the diffusion coefficient distribution (in units of r = Dmax = 1). Dashed lines indicate continuous phase transitions, and solid lines are first-order phase transitions (consistent with the convention in Ref. [49]). The dotted vertical line at ν = 2 in the phase diagram of I(y) delimits the boundary between a normal (ν ≥2) and anomalous condensate (1 < ν < 2). The calculations to generate these phase diagrams, for the more general case of W(D) a Beta distribution, are included in Appendix B.

FIG. 4. Sketch of trajectory condensation for ν > 1 in the fluid, coexistence, and saturated phases, cf. Table I. Top. Represen- tative conditioned trajectories x(s)/(yt). The insets indicate the number of runs Nt and the displacement fraction f∗carried by the largest run. Bottom. First-run laws Pt(ξ | y) on the complete axis ξ/(yt). Blue, orange, and black denote the fluid sector, condensate sector, and the Dirac atom at yt from trajectories without any switch. For their masses, see Sec. 4.
